title: A state is a prediction engine
focus: What can a spin experiment tell us?
text: Imagine preparing many identical spin one-half systems. Measuring along the vertical axis gives sixty percent plus outcomes. Have you completely identified the quantum state? Surprisingly, no. To understand why, we need the formalism: states, operators, probabilities, measurement updates, and time evolution. Our small two-level laboratory will turn those postulates into predictions you can test.

title: One state, many representations
focus: A complex vector is not a physical arrow
text: A pure state is represented by a normalized ket in a complex Hilbert space. A bra is its conjugate transpose, so the inner product includes complex conjugation. In an orthonormal two-state basis, the coefficients are probability amplitudes. Their squared magnitudes sum to one. Changing basis changes the coordinates, not the preparation. A common overall phase also leaves every measurement probability unchanged.

title: Predict: how many dimensions?
focus: Three measurement axes; how many independent basis states?
text: Pause and predict. Spin can be measured along three spatial axes. Does that make its spin Hilbert space three-dimensional? Choose between two dimensions, three dimensions, and infinitely many dimensions. Distinguish the number of possible apparatus orientations from the number of independent states needed to describe this degree of freedom.

title: Dimension counts independent states
focus: Spin-only Hilbert space: complex dimension two
text: For spin one-half alone, the answer is two. The plus and minus vertical-spin states form a complete basis. Measurements along other directions use different bases in that same space. Position and other degrees of freedom require additional structure; we have deliberately excluded them. The Bloch arrow summarizes a two-level state. It is not a tiny spinning ball or a particle trajectory.

title: An observable is an operator
focus: Physical outcomes come from the spectrum
text: An observable is represented here by a Hermitian operator. Its eigenvalues are possible results of an ideal projective measurement. Its eigenvectors, or more generally its eigenspaces, describe states with definite values. Hermiticity gives real eigenvalues. Completeness of the orthogonal spectral projectors guarantees that the probabilities for all mutually exclusive outcomes add to one.

title: The spin scale matters
focus: Pauli outcomes are dimensionless; spin has units
text: The Pauli z matrix has eigenvalues plus one and minus one. Physical z spin is h-bar divided by two times that matrix, so the measured angular momenta are plus or minus h-bar over two. H-bar is Planck's constant divided by two pi. Never silently exchange a dimensionless Pauli expectation with a physical spin value.

title: Predict: a single outcome
focus: Prepare horizontal plus; measure vertical spin
text: Prepare the horizontal plus state and measure vertical spin once. Can the detector report zero because the average vertical spin is zero? title: An average is not an allowed click
focus: Eigenvalues constrain single-shot outcomes
text: The detector reports one of the two eigenvalues, each with probability one half in this preparation. Zero is the expectation value, not a possible single-shot result. Writing an operator in its spectral form, as eigenvalue times projector summed over outcomes, makes this distinction explicit. Degenerate eigenvalues correspond to whole eigenspaces rather than a uniquely selected eigenvector.

title: The Born rule turns amplitudes into chances
focus: Project onto an eigenspace; take the squared norm
text: For an ideal measurement, the probability of an outcome is the squared length of the state projected into its eigenspace. For a nondegenerate outcome, this is the squared magnitude of the inner product with its eigenket. Amplitudes can be complex or negative. Probabilities cannot. Taking a coefficient directly as a probability can give an impossible answer.

title: Condition on the recorded outcome
focus: Projection, followed by normalization
text: Our example has vertical plus probability zero point six and vertical minus probability zero point four. Its relative phase does not appear in those two numbers, but it matters in other bases. If an outcome is recorded, the conditional post-measurement state is the projected ket divided by its norm. An impossible outcome has no conditional state; division by zero is not physics.

title: Expectation means a weighted ensemble
focus: The average can lie between allowed outcomes
text: An expectation value combines the possible outcomes with their Born probabilities. For our vertical measurement, sixty percent plus h-bar over two and forty percent minus h-bar over two give an average of zero point one h-bar. That average describes many identically prepared systems. It does not mean that each system contains a little fraction of each detector result.

title: Compute the prediction two ways
focus: Matrix product agrees with the spectral sum
text: Compute the expectation as bra, operator, ket. Then independently compute the probability-weighted eigenvalue sum. They must agree. For one thousand independent preparations, the expected number of vertical plus outcomes is six hundred, with a binomial standard deviation of about fifteen point five. A simulated histogram illustrates sampling fluctuations; it is not a claim of measured laboratory data.

title: Order can change the experiment
focus: An ignored measurement can still change later statistics
text: Prepare vertical plus. An immediate vertical measurement gives plus with certainty. Now insert a horizontal measurement and ignore its result. The resulting ensemble is an equal mixture of horizontal plus and horizontal minus. A later vertical measurement gives plus only half the time. Ignoring the record is not the same operation as omitting the apparatus.

title: Compatibility is an operator statement
focus: Commuting observables admit a common eigenbasis
text: For finite-dimensional Hermitian observables, commuting operators can be simultaneously diagonalized. Horizontal and vertical spin do not commute. Their ideal measurement order can therefore matter. But a zero expectation of their commutator in one specially chosen state does not make the commutator operator zero. Compatibility concerns the operators, not just one number calculated in one preparation.

title: Time evolution is unitary between measurements
focus: The Hamiltonian generates the change
text: For an isolated system, the Schrödinger equation generates unitary time evolution. A time-independent Hamiltonian gives an exponential operator. An energy eigenstate acquires only an overall phase, leaving time-independent-observable probabilities unchanged. A superposition of different energies accumulates relative phase, which can change interference and expectation values. Stationary does not mean that the ket has literally stopped acquiring phase.

title: Watch relative phase become measurable
focus: A z Hamiltonian rotates horizontal-spin statistics
text: Start in horizontal plus and choose the Hamiltonian proportional to the Pauli z matrix. Write the dimensionless rotation angle as omega times time. Vertical probabilities stay one half, but horizontal plus probability oscillates as cosine squared of half that angle. At a pi rotation the state is horizontal minus. Unchanged vertical statistics alone would miss this entire change.

title: A single basis leaves questions unanswered
focus: Distinct states can share identical measurement statistics
text: We can now revisit the opening puzzle. Vertical probabilities determine populations, but not the relative phase. Two different pure states can agree on those data and disagree in another basis. Measuring horizontal and transverse spin provides additional information. Inferring a state requires a model of preparation, a sufficient set of measurements, uncertainty estimates, and an honest statement of what remains undetermined.

title: Turn the postulates into an algorithm
focus: Prepare, choose, predict, update, evolve and test
text: Our laboratory represents a pure two-level state, an ideal observable and a defined sequence of operations. Normalize the state, find spectral projectors, compute probabilities, condition on recorded outcomes, and evolve between measurements. Do not apply the pure-state picture blindly to an unrecorded ensemble or a system entangled with its environment. Those cases require a broader state description.
